detailedAnswer: PECS summarizes wildcard use: use extends when you only produce values from a structure, and super when you only consume values into it, because a List of Number cannot accept a List of Integer as a subtype even though Integer is a subtype of Number. Type erasure means generic type arguments are removed at compile time, so a List of String and a List of Integer are the same class at runtime, you cannot overload methods that differ only by generic argument, and you cannot create arrays of a parameterized type directly. The compiler inserts casts and bridge methods so overriding still works after erasure, which is why reflection sometimes reveals synthetic bridge methods. When erasure loses information you need at runtime, pass an explicit Class token or a type token instead of fighting the type system.
followUps: Why can you not overload a method on List of String versus List of Integer?
How do you recover type information lost to erasure?
question: Explain PECS and type erasure, and the practical limits they place on generic code.
shortAnswer: PECS: extends for producers, super for consumers; erasure removes type arguments at runtime, so generic overloads and parameterized arrays are impossible and reflection may show bridge methods.
tips: Give one producer example and one consumer example.
Mention bridge methods — senior interviewers listen for them.
title: Generics: PECS and erasure

detailedAnswer: ConcurrentHashMap scales by striping locks across bins rather than locking the whole map, and its atomic bulk methods such as compute, merge, and forEach operate per bin, so they do not give you a consistent snapshot across the whole map. A mapping function in computeIfAbsent must be short, non-blocking, and side-effect free, because it can run while holding a bin lock and may be invoked more than once under contention, which can stall other threads or cause surprising duplicate work. Sizing matters less than in HashMap because concurrency level is a hint, not a hard segment count, but an undersized map still resizes under load, and a huge initial capacity wastes memory. For high-contention counters, prefer LongAdder over AtomicLong inside the map, and for compound multi-key updates, accept that you need an external lock or a redesign, not a single atomic map call.
followUps: Why is there no atomic operation across two keys?
When does LongAdder beat AtomicLong?
question: What are the scaling limits and traps of ConcurrentHashMap in high-contention code?
shortAnswer: It scales by bin-level locking, but compute functions run under a bin lock and may repeat, bulk operations are not whole-map atomic, and multi-key updates need external coordination.
tips: Name the computeIfAbsent trap specifically.
State plainly that no map call is atomic across two keys.
title: ConcurrentHashMap at scale

detailedAnswer: A correct parallel reduction needs an associative, stateless combiner and an identity that is truly neutral, otherwise results vary between runs depending on how work is split. Stateful intermediate operations such as sorted, distinct, and limit on an unordered stream force buffering or coordination that can erase parallel gains, and encounter order adds further coordination costs that an unordered stream avoids. Short-circuiting operations such as findAny are faster in parallel than findFirst, which must respect order. Before parallelizing, check that the source splits efficiently — a LinkedList or an iterator-based stream splits poorly — that the per-element work is large enough to outweigh splitting overhead, and that no operation blocks or mutates shared state.
followUps: Why does a parallel reduce give different answers if the combiner is not associative?
Why is findAny faster than findFirst in parallel?
question: What makes a stream reduction correct in parallel, and which operations destroy parallel performance?
shortAnswer: Parallel reduction needs an associative combiner and a true identity; stateful operations, encounter order, poor splitting, and blocking or mutating operations destroy its gains.
tips: Use associativity as the correctness test.
Mention findAny versus findFirst as the concrete ordering example.
title: Parallel stream correctness

detailedAnswer: An executor saturates in stages: tasks queue up, threads grow to the maximum, the queue fills, and then the rejection policy decides whether callers block, run the task themselves, or drop it — and the default abort policy throws RejectedExecutionException at the worst moment. A bounded queue with caller-runs or a backpressure-aware policy protects downstream systems, while an unbounded queue hides overload until memory or latency explodes. Separate executors by workload class — CPU-bound, blocking I/O, and scheduled work — so one slow dependency cannot starve everything else, and expose queue depth, active threads, and rejections as metrics with alerts. Virtual threads change the calculus for blocking I/O by making a thread per task cheap, but they do not remove the need for bounds, timeouts, and backpressure when the downstream system itself is the bottleneck.
followUps: Why is an unbounded queue more dangerous than a rejection?
When do virtual threads not solve saturation?
question: How do you design an executor so overload degrades gracefully instead of crashing the service?
shortAnswer: Bound the queue, choose an explicit rejection policy, separate executors by workload, and alert on queue depth and rejections; virtual threads help blocking I/O but do not remove downstream limits.
tips: Walk through the saturation stages in order.
Warn that an unbounded queue hides overload until it is too late.
title: Executor saturation and backpressure

detailedAnswer: Start from the symptom: long pauses point to garbage collection logs and heap sizing, a steadily growing heap points to a leak, and high CPU without progress points to a hot loop or lock contention. Enable GC logging, then read pause times, allocation rate, and promotion rate before touching flags, and take a heap dump only after confirming the heap is actually growing, since a dump freezes or slows the process. Analyze the dump for the largest retained objects and their shortest paths to GC roots, which usually reveal a static cache, a listener never deregistered, or an unbounded collection. Metaspace growth points instead to classloader leaks, often from repeated redeploys, while native memory growth points outside the heap entirely. Fix the retention cause, then tune the collector; tuning flags around a leak only postpones the outage.
followUps: How do you distinguish a leak from a heap that is too small?
What does growth in Metaspace, rather than the heap, suggest?
question: Production heap usage climbs until the service restarts. How do you diagnose it?
shortAnswer: Confirm growth with GC logs, identify whether it is heap, Metaspace, or native memory, then analyze a heap dump for dominant retained objects and their paths to GC roots and fix the retention cause.
tips: Order the answer: confirm, locate, analyze, fix — not flags first.
Name the usual suspects: static caches, unremoved listeners, unbounded collections.
title: Diagnosing a production memory leak

detailedAnswer: Spring AOP and @Transactional work through proxies: a call from outside the bean goes through the proxy, which starts a transaction or applies advice, while a call from one method of the bean to another bypasses the proxy entirely, so the annotation on the called method is silently ignored. The same applies to private methods, which proxies cannot intercept, and to final classes or methods with JDK dynamic proxies. The fixes are to restructure so the transactional method is called through another bean, to self-inject the proxy, or to use AspectJ weaving when proxy limits are truly unacceptable. This also explains why @Transactional on a method that only calls another method in the same class appears to do nothing, and why a rollback only happens for unchecked exceptions by default unless rollbackFor is configured.
followUps: Why does @Transactional not work on a private method?
How do you make a self-call go through the proxy?
question: Why does @Transactional sometimes silently do nothing, and how do proxies explain it?
shortAnswer: Proxies only intercept external calls, so self-invocation and private methods bypass @Transactional; call through another bean or the proxy, and remember rollback is unchecked-only by default.
tips: Explain the proxy mechanism before the fix.
Mention rollbackFor, since it is the second half of the same interview question.
title: Spring proxies and self-invocation

detailedAnswer: Auto-configuration classes are ordered and conditional, so when two starters provide the same bean, the one whose conditions match and that is ordered first wins, and a user-defined bean of the same type normally makes auto-configuration back off via @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Conflicts usually come from an explicit @Bean that shadows the auto-configured one, a starter pulled in transitively that you did not expect, or a condition such as @ConditionalOnClass that behaves differently in tests versus production because the classpath differs. Debug with the auto-configuration report, which lists what applied, what was excluded, and why each candidate was skipped, and with the conditions evaluation report in tests. Prefer excluding a specific auto-configuration or defining a replacement bean deliberately over broad component-scan exclusions, which hide future surprises.
followUps: How do you find which starter brought in an unwanted bean?
When is excluding an auto-configuration better than overriding its bean?
question: Two starters configure the same bean and the wrong one wins. How do you diagnose and resolve it?
shortAnswer: Check conditions, ordering, and the auto-configuration report; a user bean normally backs auto-configuration off, so resolve conflicts by excluding a specific auto-configuration or defining the intended bean explicitly.
tips: Name the auto-configuration report as the first diagnostic step.
Distinguish transitive starter surprises from deliberate overrides.
title: Auto-configuration conflicts

detailedAnswer: Filters run at the servlet level, before Spring MVC dispatches, so they see every request but not the handler, while interceptors run inside Spring MVC around the handler, with access to the controller method and model, and argument resolvers and exception resolvers run even closer to the handler. Use filters for cross-cutting transport concerns such as logging and authentication headers, interceptors for handler-aware concerns such as feature flags or tenant context, and @ControllerAdvice for consistent error translation. For asynchronous handling, Callable and DeferredResult release the request thread while work completes, and WebFlux-style reactive endpoints only help when the whole downstream chain is non-blocking; wrapping a blocking call in a reactive type just moves the blockage. Idempotency for retried POSTs belongs at the API layer with an idempotency key stored with the result, not in the client retry logic alone.
followUps: Why can a filter not know which controller will handle a request?
When does async handling not improve throughput?
question: How do filters, interceptors, and async handling differ in Spring MVC, and where does idempotency belong?
shortAnswer: Filters run before dispatch without handler knowledge, interceptors run around the handler, async releases the request thread, and idempotency belongs server-side with a stored key and result.
tips: Order the layers from outermost to innermost.
Flag wrapping a blocking call in a reactive type as fake async.
title: Filters, interceptors, and async MVC

detailedAnswer: Optimistic locking with a @Version column lets concurrent updates proceed and fails the loser with an OptimisticLockException instead of silently overwriting, which suits low-contention data such as user profiles, while pessimistic locking suits high-contention resources such as inventory counts. Isolation levels trade correctness for concurrency: read committed prevents dirty reads, repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads, and serializable prevents phantoms, but each stronger level costs throughput and increases lock waits. Lost updates, phantom reads, and write skew are the anomalies to name, and the fix is usually a version column plus a retry for the loser, or a pessimistic lock for the contested row, rather than raising the global isolation level. Second-level caching helps read-heavy reference data but can serve stale entities across nodes, so it needs explicit invalidation and must never cache frequently mutated data.
followUps: When would you choose pessimistic over optimistic locking?
Why is raising the global isolation level usually the wrong fix?
question: How do you handle concurrent updates in JPA, and what do isolation levels actually buy you?
shortAnswer: Optimistic locking with @Version for low contention, pessimistic locks for hot rows, and isolation levels chosen per anomaly, not raised globally; cache only stable reference data.
tips: Pair each locking strategy with its contention profile.
Name one anomaly per isolation level instead of reciting definitions.
title: JPA locking and isolation

detailedAnswer: Two-phase commit gives strong consistency across services but couples them to a coordinator and blocks on coordinator failure, so most systems accept eventual consistency and design for it. A saga sequences local transactions with compensating actions for rollback, but compensations are not true rollbacks: they are new business operations that must themselves be idempotent and must handle partial failure. The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem by writing the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change, then relaying it asynchronously, so an event is never lost and never sent without its state change. Consumers must still be idempotent, because at-least-once delivery means duplicates are normal, and event schemas must evolve compatibly so old consumers keep working.
followUps: Why is a compensating action not the same as a rollback?
How does the outbox pattern solve the dual-write problem?
question: How do you keep data consistent across microservices without distributed transactions?
shortAnswer: Use sagas with idempotent compensations for multi-service workflows and the transactional outbox for reliable event publication, and make every consumer idempotent under at-least-once delivery.
tips: Contrast 2PC blocking with saga compensation explicitly.
Name the dual-write problem — it is the heart of the question.
title: Sagas and the transactional outbox

detailedAnswer: Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and running totals compute over a window of rows without collapsing them, so you can rank orders per customer or compute a moving average while keeping every row. Offset pagination with LIMIT and OFFSET is simple but scans and discards skipped rows, so it slows as the offset grows and can skip or repeat rows when data changes between pages. Keyset pagination, filtering on an ordered unique key such as a timestamp plus id, stays fast at any depth and is stable under inserts, but it cannot jump to an arbitrary page number. Covering indexes, which include every column a query needs, let the database answer from the index alone, but each extra index costs write performance and storage, so verify with the execution plan and measure on realistic data volumes.
followUps: Why can offset pagination skip rows when data changes?
When is a covering index worth its write cost?
question: When do window functions and keyset pagination beat GROUP BY and OFFSET pagination?
shortAnswer: Window functions rank and aggregate without collapsing rows; keyset pagination on an ordered unique key stays fast and stable at depth, while OFFSET scans skipped rows and shifts under concurrent writes.
tips: Give one window-function example and one keyset example.
State the OFFSET weakness in terms of scanning, not just slowness.
title: Window functions and keyset pagination

detailedAnswer: The task is to design an LRU cache with get and put in constant time. The idiomatic approach pairs a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency: the map gives constant-time lookup, and the list lets you move a node to the front on access and evict the tail node on overflow, both in constant time. On get, return the value and move its node to the front; on put, insert or update the node, move it to the front, and if the size exceeds capacity, remove the tail node from both the list and the map. A linked hash map in access-order mode provides this out of the box in Java, but interviewers usually want the map-plus-list structure explained, and for a concurrent version you must add locking or sharding rather than assuming the structure is thread-safe.
followUps: How would you make this cache thread-safe?
How does the design change if eviction must consider entry size, not just count?
question: Coding task: design an LRU cache with constant-time get and put. What data structures do you combine, and why?
shortAnswer: Combine a hash map for constant-time lookup with a doubly linked list for recency order: move accessed nodes to the front and evict from the tail.
tips: Explain why each structure alone is insufficient.
Mention LinkedHashMap access-order mode, then explain the underlying structure anyway.
title: Coding: LRU cache design

detailedAnswer: First, establish whether threads are blocked, deadlocked, or merely busy: thread dumps taken a few seconds apart show threads stuck in the same place for a deadlock or lock wait, versus threads moving through different code for CPU saturation. A common root cause is a thread pool exhausted by calls to a slow downstream service without timeouts, so every request thread waits and new requests queue until the service appears dead. Mitigate immediately by shedding load or restarting with bounded pools and timeouts, then fix the dependency contract: add timeouts, bulkheads per dependency, and circuit breakers, and alert on queue depth before it reaches saturation. A post-incident review should ask why the missing timeout was not caught by a checklist or test, because the same failure will recur with the next slow dependency.
followUps: How do thread dumps distinguish deadlock from CPU saturation?
What metric would have warned you before saturation?
question: Scenario: a service stops responding under normal traffic, CPU is low, and restarts only help briefly. How do you diagnose it?
shortAnswer: Low CPU plus unresponsiveness suggests thread-pool exhaustion or deadlock; compare thread dumps over time, then bound pools, add timeouts and bulkheads, and alert on queue depth.
tips: Use the low-CPU clue — it rules out a hot loop.
Name bulkheads as the structural fix, not just timeouts.
title: Scenario: thread-pool exhaustion

detailedAnswer: Records give concise immutable data carriers with automatically generated equals, hashCode, and accessors, and they suit DTOs and value objects, but they are final and cannot extend another class, so they are a poor fit for entities with evolving behaviour or frameworks that require proxies and no-arg construction. Sealed classes restrict which classes may extend them, which makes a hierarchy exhaustive and lets pattern-matching switches be checked by the compiler, and pattern matching replaces chains of instanceof checks and casts with a single readable form. Virtual threads make a thread-per-request style cheap for blocking I/O workloads, but they do not help CPU-bound work and they can pin a carrier thread when code synchronizes on a monitor. Migrate incrementally: introduce records and pattern matching where they clarify code, and adopt virtual threads only after confirming the workload is blocking I/O and the libraries used do not pin carriers.
followUps: Why are records a poor fit for JPA entities?
When does a virtual thread pin its carrier thread?
question: How do you decide where records, sealed classes, pattern matching, and virtual threads actually help?
shortAnswer: Records for immutable data carriers, sealed classes for exhaustive hierarchies, pattern matching for type dispatch, and virtual threads only for blocking I/O workloads that do not pin carriers.
tips: Give one good fit and one poor fit per feature.
Warn about carrier pinning for virtual threads — it is the current senior-level trap.
title: Modern Java: where each feature fits
